facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops is a genus of herbivorous ceratopsian dinosaur whose name means "no nose-horn face".
facts.quote: Arrhinoceratops (meaning "no nose-horn face", derived from the Ancient Greek "a-/α-" "no", rhis/ῥίς "nose" "keras/κέρας" "horn", "-ops/ὤψ" "face") is a genus of herbivorous ceratopsian dinosaur.

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops lived during the latest Campanian or earliest Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous, predating Triceratops but living at the same time as Anchiceratops.
facts.quote: It lived during the latest Campanian/earliest Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, predating its famous relative Triceratops by a few million years, although it was contemporary with Anchiceratops.

facts.statement: William Arthur Parks described Arrhinoceratops in 1925 based on a partially crushed skull that lacked lower jaws.
facts.quote: Described by William Arthur Parks in 1925, Arrhinoceratops is known from a partially crushed, slightly distorted skull which lacked the lower jaws.

facts.statement: The remains of Arrhinoceratops were collected in 1923 from the Neill's Ranch site along the Red Deer River in Alberta by a University of Toronto expedition.
facts.quote: The remains were collected from the Neill's Ranch site, along the Red Deer River in Alberta by a 1923 expedition from the University of Toronto.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen ROM 796 was found in the Horseshoe Canyon Formation dating to the latest Campanian or earliest Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: The holotype is ROM 796 (earlier ROM 5135), which was found in a layer of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation dating from the latest Campanian or perhaps earliest Maastrichtian.

facts.statement: Material found in Utah in the 1930s was named Arrhinoceratops? utahensis by Charles Whitney Gilmore in 1946, though Gilmore himself doubted the identification.
facts.quote: Other material from Utah, found in the 1930s, was posthumously named Arrhinoceratops? utahensis by Charles Whitney Gilmore in 1946.

facts.statement: Douglas A. Lawson transferred the Utah species to the genus Torosaurus in 1976, renaming it Torosaurus utahensis.
facts.quote: In 1976, Douglas A. Lawson transferred the species to Torosaurus, as a Torosaurus utahensis.

facts.statement: The sides of the neck frill are adorned by approximately nine osteoderms.
facts.quote: The sides of the frill are adorned by about nine osteoderms.

facts.statement: A pathological opening on the left squamosal of the holotype suggests the animal may have suffered a wound.
facts.quote: The left squamosal in the frill side of the holotype shows a pathological opening, perhaps the result of a wound.

facts.statement: The snout of Arrhinoceratops is short and high.
facts.quote: The snout is short and high.

facts.statement: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated the length of Arrhinoceratops at 4.5 meters and its weight at 1.3 tonnes.
facts.quote: In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated its length at 4.5 m, its weight at 1.3 tonne.

facts.statement: Some popular-science books estimate the body length of Arrhinoceratops to be 6 meters when fully grown.
facts.quote: Based on the skull some popular-science books estimate the body length to be 6 m long when fully grown.

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops lived in a wet coastal environment with warm summers and cool winters.
facts.quote: Arrhinoceratops lived in a wet coast-land with warm summers but cool winters.

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops was likely preyed upon by the dinosaur Albertosaurus.
facts.quote: It was likely preyed upon by Albertosaurus.

facts.statement: Because flowering plants were geographically limited during the Cretaceous, Arrhinoceratops likely fed on ferns, cycads, and conifers.
facts.quote: During the Cretaceous, flowering plants were "geographically limited on the landscape", and so it is likely that this dinosaur fed on the predominant plants of the era: ferns, cycads and conifers.

facts.statement: The habitat of Arrhinoceratops was densely forested.
facts.quote: Its habitat was densely forested.

facts.statement: Modern research classifies Arrhinoceratops as a member of the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
facts.quote: Modern research indicates that Arrhinoceratops is a member of the Chasmosaurinae.

facts.statement: Cladistic analyses place Arrhinoceratops close to Anchiceratops.
facts.quote: Cladistic analyses recover it close to Anchiceratops.

facts.statement: Helen Tyson concluded that Arrhinoceratops was closely related to Torosaurus and possibly its direct ancestor.
facts.quote: Tyson concluded it was closely related to Torosaurus, probably even its direct ancestor.

facts.statement: Richard Swann Lull was critical of Parks' original description in 1933, and later research by Helen Tyson confirmed that Parks made many mistakes.
facts.quote: Already Richard Swann Lull had in 1933 been politely critical of Parks' original description, and Tyson discovered that Parks had made many mistakes.

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops brachyops is the only known species of the extinct genus Arrhinoceratops, a ceratopsian dinosaur that lived in North America about 70 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Maastrichtian.
facts.quote: Arrhinoceratops brachyops (gr. "cara sin cuerno de la nariz de cara corta") es la única especie conocida del género extinto Arrhinoceratops de dinosaurio ceratopsiano ceratópsido, que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 70 millones de años, en el Maastrichtiense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The rear edge of the neck frill is slightly scalloped.
facts.quote: El borde posterior del volante está ligeramente ondulado.

facts.statement: The genus Arrhinoceratops was described by W. A. Parks in 1925.
facts.quote: Descrito por W. A. Parks en 1925

facts.statement: Fossils were found in 1923 by a University of Toronto expedition along the Red Deer River in Alberta, Canada, within the Horseshoe Canyon Formation.
facts.quote: Los restos provenían de la Formación Cañón Horseshoe, las reiveras del Río Red Deer en Alberta Canadá por una expedición de 1923 de la Universidad de Toronto

facts.statement: The holotype specimen ROM 796 dates to the late Campanian or possibly early Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: El holotipo es ROM 796 (anteriormente ROM 5135), que fue encontrado en una capa de la formación Cañón Herradura que data de la última parte del Campaniano o tal vez del Maastrichtiano temprano

facts.statement: Only one species, A. brachyops, has been described for this genus.
facts.quote: Solo una especie se ha descrito, A. brachyops

facts.statement: Material from Utah originally assigned to Arrhinoceratops by Gilmore in 1946 is now considered to belong to the genus Torosaurus.
facts.quote: Otro material previamente asignado al género proveniente de Utah por Gilmore en 1946, que originalmente llamó A. utahensis?, es hoy considerado un Torosaurus

facts.statement: Douglas A. Lawson transferred the species to the genus Torosaurus in 1976.
facts.quote: En 1976, Douglas A. Lawson transfiere la especie a Torosaurus , como utahensis Torosaurus

facts.statement: Very little fossil material of A. brachyops has been found besides the holotype skull.
facts.quote: Aparte del cráneo holotipo poco material fósil de A. brachyops ha sido encontrado

facts.statement: Specimen ROM 1439 was provisionally assigned to the genus by Helen Tyson in 1981 but was later transferred to Torosaurus by Andrew Farke in 2007.
facts.quote: En 1981 Helen Tyson en una revisión del género, asignó provisionalmente espécimen ROM 1439, pero en 2007 Andrew Farke trasladó a esta Torosaurus

facts.statement: The name Arrhinoceratops is derived from Greek words meaning "no," "nose," "horn," and "face."
facts.quote: El nombre deriva del griego "a-/α-" "no", rhino-/ρινο- "nariz" "cerat-/κερατ-" "cuerno", "-ops/ωψ" "cara"

facts.statement: The original describer, W. A. Parks, was an entomologist who made several errors in his description.
facts.quote: Parks, un entomólogo, había cometido muchos errores

facts.statement: A notable error by Parks was claiming the lack of a separate prenasal bone for the horn was unique, when it is actually normal for ceratopsids.
facts.quote: El más notable de ellos fue que el rasgo que dio nombre al género, la falta de una osificación por separado de un hueso epinasal para la nariz de cuerno, de hecho es normal para los ceratópsidos

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops belongs to the subfamily Ceratopsinae, formerly known as Chasmosaurinae, within the family Ceratopsia.
facts.quote: Arrhinoceratops pertenece a Ceratopsinae, previamente conocidos como Chasmosaurinae, dentro de Ceratopsia

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops is closely related to the genera Torosaurus, Chasmosaurus, and Pentaceratops.
facts.quote: Está cercanamente relacionado con Torosaurus, Chasmosaurus y Pentaceratops

facts.statement: Helen Tyson concluded that Arrhinoceratops was closely related to Torosaurus, possibly even its direct ancestor.
facts.quote: Tyson llegó a la conclusión que estaba estrechamente relacionado con Torosaurus, probablemente incluso su antepasado directo

facts.statement: Modern research indicates that Arrhinoceratops is a member of the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
facts.quote: La investigación moderna indica que Arrhinoceratops es un miembro de Chasmosaurinae

facts.statement: Cladistic analyses place Arrhinoceratops near the genus Anchiceratops.
facts.quote: Análisis cladisticos lo ubican cerca de Anchiceratops

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops lived from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, approximately 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: The parent group of Arrhinoceratops is the subfamily Chasmosaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Chasmosaurinae

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops belongs to the family Ceratopsidae.
facts.quote: Family: Ceratopsidae

facts.statement: Arrhinoceratops is classified within the class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Arrhinoceratops in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 3
